title: Sharing the Magic: How to Build Employee Commitment From Day One
author: Kurt Mueller
source: Rookie to Pro: The Hidden Side of Leadership (kurtmueller.substack.com), October 23, 2026
summary: Kurt Mueller draws on his years at Walt Disney World to argue that onboarding should explain why a new employee's work matters before it teaches how to do the job. He describes the 'Traditions' orientation, in which every new Cast Member, regardless of position, learns the company's heritage, shared purpose and values, and only afterwards moves to role-specific training. He adds a leadership lesson: leaders are expected to develop people, using the C.O.A.C.H. acronym (Care, Observe, Act, Communicate, Help). Culture, he says, is what employees experience after orientation, not only what they hear in it. He closes with a five-step skill builder and a two-minute orientation opening that any manager can use. The evidence is anecdotal and drawn from a single employer, but the practical advice is concrete and easy to apply.
points: Purpose comes first: explaining why the work matters and who benefits builds belonging before any procedure is taught.
Making values visible through everyday decisions turns an orientation message into lived culture.
The C.O.A.C.H. model gives leaders five developmental duties: care, observe, act, communicate and help.
Visible advancement matters, since roughly three in five Disney World leaders began in hourly roles.
A two-minute opening that names why the team exists, who depends on it and how the newcomer contributes is a low-cost way to start.
quotes: Before you teach new employees how to do their jobs, help them understand why their work matters.
Most organizations begin onboarding with policies, procedures, paperwork, and job-specific training.
Everyone, regardless of position, is introduced to Disney’s heritage, shared purpose, values, and expectations.
Leaders are expected to develop their Cast Members, not simply supervise their performance.
Culture isn’t simply what employees hear during orientation. It’s what they experience afterward.
Your objective: Help the new employee recognize that they’re joining something worth contributing to—not simply filling a position.
